text: Ekalavya's Thumb: Why Can Someone Who Refused to Teach You Still Demand That You Give Up Your Skill?
Ekalavya came before Drona and asked to learn archery.

Drona was a renowned teacher, responsible for training the young princes. Ekalavya, however, did not belong to their circle. He was a Nishada prince, from a community the established order kept at a distance.
Drona refused him.
The reason was not merely that the classroom had no space left.
In the order the story presents, accepting such a student would disturb the existing hierarchy. It might also threaten Drona's promise to Arjuna: to make him an archer without equal.
Ekalavya left.
He did not give up learning.

He made a clay image of Drona, treated it as his teacher, and practiced alone in the forest. No formal instruction, no fellow pupils, no corrections from Drona. Through his own repeated practice, he developed astonishing skill.
Later, the princes encountered a dog in the forest. Seven arrows had closed its mouth without killing it outright. Ekalavya was the archer.
The young men marveled at the precision and were shaken by such ability.
Ekalavya told them:
I am Drona's pupil.
Word reached Arjuna.
Arjuna remembered his teacher's promise. He asked Drona:
Did you not say that no pupil would surpass me?
So Drona went to see Ekalavya.
Ekalavya still regarded him as his teacher and welcomed him respectfully. Drona said that, since Ekalavya was his pupil, he owed his teacher a payment.
Ekalavya was willing to give anything.
Drona asked for the thumb of his right hand.
Ekalavya immediately cut off his thumb and gave it to Drona.
He did not lose all ability to shoot, but he could no longer maintain his former speed and skill.
Arjuna was finally reassured.
Drona had kept his promise to one student.
The price was paid by another whom he had never accepted.
The sharpest point of this story is not merely that someone lost a thumb.
It is that, at two different moments, Drona adopted two mutually contradictory relationships.
When Ekalavya asked to study, he said:
You are not my student.
When Ekalavya's ability became a threat to Arjuna, he said:
Since you are my student, you owe me a teacher's payment.
He refused a teacher's responsibilities, then claimed a teacher's rights after the skill had been developed.
This makes the title “teacher” something more than an expression of respect.
It becomes a claim that reaches into someone else's body and future.
Of course, Drona did not invent this relationship entirely on his own.
Ekalavya really had made a clay image of him.
He really had treated Drona as his teacher without obtaining his consent, and had told others he was Drona's pupil.
So we can ask in return:
Can someone borrow another person's name, image, and standing to establish an identity as a learner, yet wholly deny that person's connection to that identity?
This is a real question.
Admiration does not arise from nothing.

Ekalavya may have found direction in the archery tradition, reputation, and ideal of training that Drona represented. Even without direct lessons, he did not live in a world wholly unrelated to Drona.
But “having a source” and “being owned” are still not the same thing.
Being inspired by someone can give rise to gratitude.
Borrowing someone's methods may create a responsibility to acknowledge their source.
Publicly claiming to be someone's pupil may also require answering whether that description is true.
But none of this automatically entails:
That the person respected therefore owns all the abilities the learner later develops.
Still less does it mean that, without providing training, bearing risks, or even accepting the person, he may demand the learner surrender the bodily condition that makes their excellence possible.
If respect could generate such unlimited rights, the deepest respect would make people easiest to possess.
Ekalavya offered his thumb of his own accord.
That makes the story harder.
Had Drona simply cut off his hand by force, we could easily identify what had happened.
But Ekalavya did not resist.
He did not even bargain. He saw his teacher's demand as an obligation he ought to fulfill, and acted at once.
Is this willingness enough to make the demand just?
A person can, of course, voluntarily bear an enormous cost.
We cannot declare that the action is not theirs at all simply because we disapprove. That would take their decision away once more, in another way.
But willingness does not mean the person making the demand no longer has to give reasons.
Especially where a powerful difference in status exists, a demand can be almost impossible to refuse even without a direct threat.
Ekalavya had already placed Drona in the position of teacher.
His respect for that position was precisely what enabled Drona to make the demand.
So the question most worth asking is not:
Was he willing?
But:
Why does a person's sincere respect for an authority give that authority greater power to use that respect to demand that he harm himself?
A demand cannot escape judgment merely because it is obeyed.
Obedience may demonstrate someone's commitment.
It may also show that an order has entered so deeply into them that they cannot understand “no” as an answer still permitted to them.
Drona also had a commitment of his own.
He had promised Arjuna to make him an archer without equal.
Teachers should take their promises to students seriously.
But some promises cannot be justly fulfilled from the outset.
“I will do my best to develop your abilities” is a promise a teacher can undertake.
“I will ensure that no one in the world is better than you” is different.
Because fulfilling the second promise does not depend only on the teacher and student.
It also requires that every other person who might emerge must not surpass him.
Once someone outside the promise develops greater skill, the teacher is left with two choices:
Admit that he cannot guarantee Arjuna will always be first.
Or push others down so that the original promise continues to appear fulfilled.
Drona chose the latter.
He did not make Arjuna stronger.
He made Ekalavya weaker.
This exposes the real shape of many competitive promises.
Sometimes people say they are protecting someone's position, but what they actually do is not increase that person's ability; it is restrict other people's possibilities.
If a promise can be fulfilled only by damaging a third person, what first needs reassessment may not be that person's growth, but the promise itself.
Nor can we leave the hunting dog out of the story.
Closing the dog's mouth with seven arrows displayed Ekalavya's astonishing skill. It also showed that this skill had entered the real world and did not exist only in harmless practice.
He is not someone persecuted solely for his talent who has never done anything worth questioning.
The greater the ability, the more one must answer for how it is used.
If his archery creates real danger, the community can certainly discuss limits, responsibility, and protection.
But limiting a capability and destroying someone's capability are not the same thing.
Responding to a particular harm is also different from weakening someone in advance to protect another person's first place.
What happened to the dog cannot justify Drona's demand.
It only reminds us not to rewrite Ekalavya as a modern saint without any complexity in order to criticize injustice.
Acknowledging that someone has been treated unjustly does not make everything they do right.
Likewise, someone's past conduct being open to criticism does not give authority the right to do whatever it likes with them.
An educational relationship can all too easily generate a gentle form of ownership.
The teacher provides knowledge, opportunities, training, and recognition.
The student grows through them.
After that growth, the teacher may naturally feel:
There is a part of me in your ability.
In a sense, that is true.
Human growth is almost never accomplished alone. We use language, methods, and questions preserved by others, and receive guidance from particular teachers.
Gratitude for that help acknowledges a real relationship.
But the deeper the relationship, the more important it is to separate two judgments:
You have something to do with my having come this far.
Therefore, from now on I must go where you decide for me.
The first can be genuine gratitude.
The second turns education into ownership of a future.

A real teacher gains a sense of achievement from a student's growing ability and may expect respect for the relationship they have formed together. But having helped someone grow does not entitle the teacher to demand back the part that enables that person to move forward independently.
Drona had not even done the first part.
He had not trained Ekalavya, yet he claimed more extreme rights of demand than many actual teachers.
That is why this story cuts so sharply.
Ekalavya treated the clay image as a teacher and finally gave his thumb to the living man.
The clay image had not rejected him.
Nor had it taught him.
What truly shaped his ability was his own practice, time, and body, and his trust in the position of an ideal teacher.
When the living man appeared before him, that position suddenly acquired a voice.
It said:
Hand your ability back.
But that ability had never been handed over by Drona in the first place.
So there was nothing to “give back.”
What a rejected person later learns still has sources, of course. They remain responsible for its uses and consequences and may still owe acknowledgment of whose name they borrowed.
But a source is not ownership.
Admiration is not a blank check.
A student's willingness to call someone a teacher does not let that person claim a teacher's rights without shouldering the responsibilities they once refused.
At the end of the story, Arjuna's first place is preserved.
But that place will forever carry another person's thumb.
Perhaps excellence truly worth possessing should not depend on other people being forced to remain less than they could fully become.
And someone truly worthy of being called a teacher should not demand that a student prove loyalty through mutilation just as the student's own abilities finally grow.

*Textual basis: the Ekalavya story in the Sambhava Parva of the Mahabharata's Adi Parva. This essay preserves the full chain of events: Drona's refusal to accept him, Ekalavya's clay image and independent study, the hunting-dog episode, Arjuna's questioning of the earlier promise, and Drona's demand for the right thumb. It does not simply equate the ancient Nishada identity with any modern category, nor treat the demand itself as beyond judgment because Ekalavya offered the thumb voluntarily.*
